steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Experiments test cause-and-effect by manipulating the independent variable (IV) and measuring the dependent variable (DV) while controlling extraneous variables. Types: lab (high control, low ecological validity), field (natural setting, lower control), natural (IV not manipulated), quasi (pre-existing groups).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Observations record behaviour without manipulation. Naturalistic: in a natural setting with no intervention. Controlled: some variables regulated. Covert: participants unaware. Overt: participants aware. Participant: researcher joins the group. Non-participant: researcher observes from outside.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Correlations measure the relationship between two variables without establishing causation. Positive correlation: both variables increase together. Negative: one increases as the other decreases. Zero: no relationship. Correlation does NOT mean causation.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Sampling methods: random (everyone has equal chance), systematic (every nth person), stratified (proportional representation of subgroups), opportunity (whoever is available), volunteer (self-selected). Each has strengths and limitations.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe the different types of experiment used in psychological research and evaluate their strengths and weaknesses. | Explain why correlation does not equal causation, using an example from psychology. | Compare random sampling with opportunity sampling, evaluating the strengths and limitations of each.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Lab experiment = high control, low ecological validity. Field = low control, high ecological validity. Correlation does NOT equal causation - always mention the third variable problem. Operationalise your variables: don't just measure 'memory', measure 'number of words recalled from a list of 20'.
